# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# facett_osm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-osm/0.1.10/facett_osm/

## Expand description

**facett-osm** — read **OSM GeoParquet** (the `osm2geoparquet` / katana-osm
output) into facett geometry. Each row’s `geometry` column is **WKB** — a
`Point` for nodes, a `LineString`/`Polygon` for ways — which we decode to
`(lon, lat)` points and hand to [ facett_map::MapView](https://docs.rs/facett-map/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_map/struct.MapView.html). This is how facett
gets real OSM data (millions of points) for the map component + its tests.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_wkb.html)- wkb
- Decode a WKB geometry blob, appending every `(lon, lat)`vertex to`out`. Handles Point (1), LineString (2), Polygon (3); ignores Z/M + SRID flags.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_wkb_coords.html)- wkb_ - coords
- Decode a single WKB blob into **one geometry’s**`(lon, lat)`vertices (Point → 1 vertex, LineString → its line, Polygon → its exterior ring), preserving the geometry as a unit (unlike`decode_wkb``read_ways``katana_osm_shared::geometry::decode_coords`.
- [map_](https://docs.rs/fn.map_view.html)- view
- Read a GeoParquet straight into a `facett_map::MapView`
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_points.html)- points
- Read up to `max``(lon, lat)`points from a GeoParquet file’s`geometry`(WKB) column. Works on`osm2geoparquet`’s`nodes.parquet`(Points) and`ways.parquet`(LineStrings → their vertices).
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_points_bytes.html)- points_ - bytes
- Like `read_points`**in-memory**GeoParquet (the bytes of a`nodes.parquet`). This is the filesystem-free path the wasm web demo uses: it`include_bytes!`s a clipped region into the binary and decodes it here (the browser has no`std::fs`). Any`Into<Bytes>`works (`&'static [u8]`,`Vec<u8>`).
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_ways.html)- ways
- Read **ways**(LineString / Polygon geometries) from an`osm2geoparquet``ways.parquet`— the SAME WKB`geometry`column`read_points``tags`column for styling. Each row → a`facett_map::Way``(lon, lat)`, projected to Mercator, classified by its OSM tags through`theme`.`max`caps the number of ways (0 = unlimited). Rows with <2 vertices are skipped (graceful — no panic on a degenerate geometry).
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_ways_bytes.html)- ways_ - bytes
- Like `read_ways`**in-memory**`ways.parquet`(the bytes the wasm web demo`include_bytes!`s — no filesystem in the browser).

## Expand description

autoconf-rs-cli shared library.

Provides the CLI argument parsing harness used by all 8 Autoconf binaries. Each binary is a thin wrapper that delegates to autoconf-rs-core.

- Common CLI options shared across Autoconf tools.

- Read a file into a String, or return stdin contents if path is “-”.
- [read_](https://docs.rs/fn.read_stdin.html)- stdin
- Read all of stdin into a String.

–mode=compile CC … -c src -o obj.lo   -> .libs/obj.o (PIC) + obj.o + obj.lo descriptor
–mode=link    CC … -o lib.la objs     -> .libs/lib.a (static) + .libs/lib.so (shared) + lib.la

–mode=install / –mode=clean            -> best-effort copy / rm macro_overrides  m4 macro definitions injected AFTER aclocal.m4 (so they override the project’s third-party
definitions) and BEFORE configure.ac. autoconf-rs cannot yet correctly expand some standard
third-party macros (notably pkg.m4’s PKG_CHECK_MODULES, whose internals leak
`pkg_default`/`glib_minimum` -> shell syntax errors). We replace them with clean, self-contained
shell that does the real work: run pkg-config at configure time, set PFX_CFLAGS/PFX_LIBS, and
record `@PFX_CFLAGS@`/`@PFX_LIBS@` substitutions into conf_subst.sed (consumed when config files
are created, mirroring confdefs.h -> config.h).

# facett_map3d - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-map3d/0.1.10/facett_map3d/

## Expand description

**facett-map3d** — a **3D map viewer**: the 2D OSM vector basemap
([ facett_map::Way](https://docs.rs/facett-map/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_map/struct.Way.html))

**extruded into 3D**. Building / area footprints become

**prisms**(a closed ring lifted to a height), line ways become flat

**ribbons**laid on the ground, and the whole map sits on a

**terrain plane**. A camera

**orbits**(yaw about Y + a fixed tilt) like

[, so the city reads as a solid, lit, slowly-turning model.](https://docs.rs/struct.RabbitLogo3D.html)

`facett_graph3d::RabbitLogo3D`Two render paths share one [ Facet::ui](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html#tymethod.ui) — the same contract as facett-map and
facett-graph3d:

- **CPU painter**(default, always available, headless-testable) — every extruded triangle is projected (orbit yaw + tilt),- **back-face culled**,- **depth sorted**(painter’s algorithm), and shaded by- `normal·light`. egui tessellates them, so a host with no wgpu RenderState still gets a real lit 3D map. Never panics.
- **wgpu fast path**(feature- `wgpu`) — reuses facett-graph3d’s depth-tested [- `facett_graph3d::logo3d::gpu`] pipeline for the- **znippy rabbit logo overlay**(the spinning mascot in the corner). The basemap prisms always draw on the CPU painter (the headless self-test path), so the GPU is never required.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-synthetic-3d-fixture-is-the-znippy-rabbit-not-squares)The synthetic 3D fixture is the **znippy rabbit** (not squares)

When the host has no real OSM data, [ Map3D::synthetic](https://docs.rs/struct.Map3D.html#method.synthetic) builds the basemap by

**extruding the znippy rabbit silhouette**(

[) — each rabbit loop (body / head / ears) becomes a prism — and pins a 3D](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/rabbit/index.html)

`facett_core::rabbit`[as the logo overlay. So the fixture is a 3D rabbit-shaped skyline, never a placeholder cube.](https://docs.rs/struct.RabbitLogo3D.html)

The camera orbits a- **target**point on spherical coordinates (azimuth + elevation + distance), like three.js- `OrbitControls`/- `camera-controls`and Blender’s turntable: drag to orbit, wheel to- **dolly toward the cursor**, middle/shift-drag to- **pan**, and snap to canonical- **view-angle presets**(top-down / iso / oblique / front).

- [lod](https://docs.rs/lod/index.html)
- Altitude / LOD lever + the `METRES_PER_DESIGN_UNIT`calibration (the headline`< 300 m → reflective water`trigger). Pure CPU, inject-assert-testable.**Altitude / LOD lever + the metre calibration**— the single CPU lever that turns the camera’s design-unit dolly distance into a real-world**altitude in metres**, then resolves a`LodTier``< 300 m → reflective water`rule is just one threshold of this lever.
- [sky](https://docs.rs/sky/index.html)
- Sun + sky lighting model (Phase 1) shared by the GPU PBR shader + CPU painter.
**Sun + sky lighting model**(Phase 1) — the single source of truth for the directional sun, its colour/intensity, and the sky/ambient tint, shared by the GPU PBR shader (`map3d.wgsl`) and the CPU painter so both render paths agree.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [clip_](https://docs.rs/fn.clip_poly_to_rect.html)- poly_ - to_ - rect
- **Sutherland–Hodgman**clip of a triangle to an axis-aligned- `rect`— the CPU painter’s- **scissor**.- **Moved to**(CONS-CORE Phase A, step 3) and re-exported here so map3d’s public API + its regression fence (- `facett_core::render::cpu::scissor`- `clip_pipeline`/- `frustum_scissor`/- `no_spokes`/- `near_plane_probe`/- `gpu_scissor`) are unchanged. The move is behavior-preserving.- **Sutherland–Hodgman**clip of a triangle (- `tri`) to an axis-aligned- `rect`, returning the clipped convex polygon’s vertices (3..=7 of them) or an empty Vec when the triangle lies wholly outside the rect. This is the CPU painter’s- **scissor**: it geometrically confines every face to the widget rect so nothing a 3D/2D pass paints can land outside the component’s own rectangle — independent of whether the host renderer applies the egui clip_rect as a GPU scissor.
- [clip_](https://docs.rs/fn.clip_tri_frustum.html)- tri_ - frustum
- **Full view-space FRUSTUM clip**(the real fix for the smear) — Sutherland–Hodgman of a triangle against all FIVE relevant frustum planes BEFORE the perspective divide: the near plane- `z >= near`AND the four side planes- `|cx| <= cz·sx`,- `|cy| <= cz·sy`(with- `sx`,- `sy`the projection’s per-axis NDC slopes — for- `project_view`’s focal =- `half_h`,- `sy = 1`,- `sx = half_w/half_h`).
- [clip_](https://docs.rs/fn.clip_tri_near.html)- tri_ - near
- **View-space near-plane clip**(step 1 of the part-step decomposition) — Sutherland–Hodgman clip of a single view-space triangle against the half-space- `z >= near`, returning the clipped convex polygon’s view-space vertices (0 when the whole triangle sits on/behind the eye, 3 when untouched, 4 when one vertex was behind and split). This runs- **before**the perspective divide so no surviving vertex ever divides by a near-zero / negative depth — the geometric replacement for the old “near-singularity spoke reject” + “screen-extent guard” heuristics that let off-axis near faces smear thousands of px off the rect.
- [ink_](https://docs.rs/fn.ink_outside_rect.html)- outside_ - rect
- **Sutherland–Hodgman**clip of a triangle to an axis-aligned- `rect`— the CPU painter’s- **scissor**.- **Moved to**(CONS-CORE Phase A, step 3) and re-exported here so map3d’s public API + its regression fence (- `facett_core::render::cpu::scissor`- `clip_pipeline`/- `frustum_scissor`/- `no_spokes`/- `near_plane_probe`/- `gpu_scissor`) are unchanged. The move is behavior-preserving. The scissor- **oracle**(- `scissor.ink_outside_rect`): count the vertices of the- *scissored*polygons that still land outside- `rect`(beyond- `eps`). A correct scissor leaves- **0**— this is the bug oracle the spec’s clip stage emits (- `ink_outside_rect == 0`). Pure, so both the emit path and tests call it.
- [scissor_](https://docs.rs/fn.scissor_report.html)- report
- **Scissor oracle**(step 7) — measure how far the faces overshoot the widget rect- *before*the rect-scissor confines them, and confirm the clipped output never lands outside. Returns- `(raw_overshoot_px, clipped_escapes)`:

# blueprint_tangle_aggregation_svc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/blueprint-tangle-aggregation-svc/0.2.0-alpha.10/blueprint_tangle_aggregation_svc/

## Expand description

Tangle BLS Signature Aggregation Service

A simple HTTP service that collects BLS signatures from operators, aggregates them once threshold is met, and provides the aggregated result for submission to the Tangle contract.

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

```
Operator 1 ──┐
Operator 2 ──┼──▶ Aggregation Service ──▶ Aggregated Result
Operator 3 ──┘         │
                       ▼
                 Tangle Contract
```
[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

[§](https://docs.rs#starting-the-service)Starting the service

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use blueprint_tangle_aggregation_svc::{AggregationService, api, ServiceConfig};
use std::sync::Arc;
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let service = Arc::new(AggregationService::new(ServiceConfig::default()));
    let app = api::router(service);
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:8080").await.unwrap();
    axum::serve(listener, app).await.unwrap();
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#api-endpoints)API Endpoints

- `POST /v1/tasks/init`- Initialize an aggregation task
- `POST /v1/tasks/submit`- Submit a signature
- `POST /v1/tasks/status`- Get task status
- `POST /v1/tasks/aggregate`- Get aggregated result

[§](https://docs.rs#operator-flow)Operator Flow

- Someone (often the first operator) initializes the task
- Each operator signs the output and submits their signature
- Once threshold is met, anyone can fetch the aggregated result
- Submit the aggregated result to the Tangle contract

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use persistence::`- [FilePersistence](https://docs.rs/persistence/struct.FilePersistence.html);
- `pub use persistence::`- [NoPersistence](https://docs.rs/persistence/struct.NoPersistence.html);
- `pub use persistence::`- [PersistedTaskState](https://docs.rs/persistence/struct.PersistedTaskState.html);
- `pub use persistence::`- [PersistedThresholdType](https://docs.rs/persistence/enum.PersistedThresholdType.html);

# bamboo_agent - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bamboo-agent/2026.7.3/bamboo_agent/

## Expand description

Bamboo - A fully self-contained AI agent backend framework

Bamboo provides a complete backend system for AI agents, including:

- Built-in HTTP/HTTPS server (Actix-web)
- Agent execution loop with tool support
- LLM provider integrations (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, GitHub Copilot)
- Session management and persistence
- Workflow and slash command systems
- Process management for external tools

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- **Dual mode**: Binary (standalone server) or library (embedded)
- **Unified directory**: All data in the Bamboo data directory (default- `${HOME}/.bamboo`)
- **Production-ready**: Built-in CORS, rate limiting, security headers

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

[§](https://docs.rs#binary-mode)Binary Mode

`bamboo serve --port 9562 --data-dir "$HOME/.bamboo"`[§](https://docs.rs#library-mode)Library Mode

# crumbex 0.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/crumbex/0.2.0

# crumbex

**Polyglot code-intelligence in a single Rust binary.** Parse once, read surgically, map
the architecture, enforce the contract — with zero LLM in the core.

Crumbex parses a codebase **once** into a shared tree-sitter index and serves several
independent, opt-in layers over it: symbol search + surgical line reading, a dependency
graph (god modules, import cycles, communities), a function-level call graph, a cross-repo
service **atlas** with multi-hop feature paths, and cross-repo API **contract** enforcement.
Each layer is a Cargo feature — you pay binary weight only for what you compile.

## Install

```
```
Installs the `crumbex` binary. Building the tree-sitter grammars needs a C compiler (MSVC
Build Tools on Windows, clang via Xcode CLT on macOS, gcc/clang on Linux).

## Usage

Run `crumbex --help` for the full command list.

## Languages

TypeScript · TSX · JavaScript · Go · Python · Rust · Ruby. Adding a language is one tree-sitter grammar plus a query file — the engine never changes.

## Documentation & source

Full guide, worked examples, and roadmap: [https://github.com/Razielini/crumbex](https://github.com/Razielini/crumbex).

## License

Dual-licensed under **MIT OR Apache-2.0**, at your option.

---

# base64_ng_tokio - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64-ng-tokio/1.3.0/base64_ng_tokio/

## Expand description

Optional Tokio async helpers for `base64-ng`.

The crate provides two API tiers:

- read-all/write-all convenience functions, with `*_limited`variants for peer-controlled request or frame boundaries.
- manual `AsyncRead``EncoderReader``DecoderReader`

The streaming readers are implemented as explicit state machines. They do
not use `async fn` internally, so cancellation can only leave data in the
adapter’s fixed pending/output buffers; those buffers are cleared on drop.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

The read-all helpers use temporary `Vec<u8>` allocations and the normal
strict decode path. They wipe those temporary vectors before returning, but
they are not constant-time-oriented token validators or high-assurance
secret decoders. For secret-bearing async frames, collect a bounded frame
under the application’s approved memory policy and decode through
`base64_ng::ct`, staged CT decode, `base64-ng-derive`, or
`base64-ng-sanitization`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Decoder](https://docs.rs/struct.DecoderReader.html)- Reader
- Async reader that streams Base64 input as decoded bytes.
- [Encoder](https://docs.rs/struct.EncoderReader.html)- Reader
- Async reader that streams raw bytes as Base64.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_reader_to_writer.html)- reader_ - to_ - writer
- Reads all Base64 bytes from `reader`, decodes them, and writes decoded bytes.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_reader_to_writer_limited.html)- reader_ - to_ - writer_ - limited
- Reads at most `max_input_len`Base64 bytes from`reader`, decodes them, and writes decoded bytes.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_to_vec.html)- to_ - vec
- Decodes `input`into an owned byte vector.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_reader_to_writer.html)- reader_ - to_ - writer
- Reads all bytes from `reader`, encodes them, and writes the encoded output.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_reader_to_writer_limited.html)- reader_ - to_ - writer_ - limited
- Reads at most `max_input_len`bytes from`reader`, encodes them, and writes the encoded output.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_to_vec.html)- to_ - vec
- Encodes `input`into an owned byte vector.

# base64_ng_subtle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/base64-ng-subtle/1.3.0/base64_ng_subtle/

## Expand description

Optional `subtle::ConstantTimeEq` integration for `base64-ng`.

The core `base64-ng` package stays zero-runtime-dependency. This companion
crate exists for applications that already admit `subtle` and want a
reviewed comparison primitive at the protocol boundary.

Length is treated as public. Mismatched lengths return
[`subtle::Choice::from(0)`] immediately. Use fixed-size protocol tokens when
length must not vary. When the length itself is secret, compare fixed-size
arrays or fixed-width protocol buffers directly with
[ subtle::ConstantTimeEq](https://docs.rs/subtle/2.6.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/subtle/trait.ConstantTimeEq.html) instead of this public-length helper.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Subtle](https://docs.rs/trait.SubtleEqExt.html)- EqExt
- Extension trait for comparing `base64-ng`buffers with`subtle`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [subtle_](https://docs.rs/fn.subtle_ct_eq_public_len.html)- ct_ - eq_ - public_ - len
- Compares two byte slices with public length.

# bamboo_server - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bamboo-server/2026.7.3/bamboo_server/

## Expand description

Unified HTTP server consolidating web_service and agent/server

This module provides a single, consolidated server implementation that:

- Eliminates the proxy pattern from web_service
- Provides direct provider access without HTTP callbacks
- Unifies state management across all endpoints
- Supports all API routes (agent, OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini)

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

The server is organized into several key components:

- **app_state**: Unified state management with direct provider access
- **config**: CORS and security header configuration
- **metrics**: Unified metrics infrastructure
- **handlers**: Agent API handlers (chat, execute, events, etc.)
- **controllers**: Multi-provider API controllers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini)
- **services**: Business logic services
- **routes**: Route configuration for all API endpoints
- **server**: Entry points for running the server

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use std::path::PathBuf;
use bamboo_server::run;
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), String> {
    let app_data_dir = PathBuf::from("/path/to/bamboo-data-dir");
    run(app_data_dir, 3456).await
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#server-modes)Server Modes

The server supports three modes:

[§](https://docs.rs#1-desktop-mode-default)1. Desktop Mode (Default)

Binds to localhost only, No rate limiting. Perfect for local development.

```
use std::path::PathBuf;
use bamboo_server::run;
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), String> {
    let data_dir = PathBuf::from("./.bamboo");
    run(data_dir, 9562).await
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#2-docker-mode)2. Docker Mode

Custom bind address with rate limiting. For containerized deployments.

```
use std::path::PathBuf;
use bamboo_server::run_with_bind;
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), String> {
    let data_dir = PathBuf::from("./.bamboo");
    run_with_bind(data_dir, 9562, "0.0.0.0").await
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#3-production-mode-with-frontend)3. Production Mode with Frontend

Serves static files alongside API. Full production setup.

```
use std::path::PathBuf;
use bamboo_server::run_with_bind_and_static;
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), String> {
    let data_dir = PathBuf::from("./.bamboo");
    run_with_bind_and_static(
        data_dir,
        9562,
        "0.0.0.0",
        Some(PathBuf::from("./dist")),
    )
    .await
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#route-organization)Route Organization

[§](https://docs.rs#agent-routes-apiv1)Agent Routes (/api/v1/*)

Core agent functionality: chat, execute, events, metrics, MCP.

[§](https://docs.rs#openai-routes-v1)OpenAI Routes (/v1/*)

OpenAI-compatible API for tool integration.

[§](https://docs.rs#anthropic-routes-anthropicv1)Anthropic Routes (/anthropic/v1/*)

Anthropic Claude API compatible endpoints.

[§](https://docs.rs#gemini-routes-geminiv1beta)Gemini Routes (/gemini/v1beta/*)

Google Gemini API compatible endpoints.

# measurements 0.11.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/measurements/0.11.1

# Type-safe units of measure for Rust

### Why should I care? I already have numbers...

Working with units can be very error prone. If one person is working in feet and one person is working in meters, what happens?

Doing all of your math in raw numerical types can be unsafe and downright confusing. What can we do to help?

### Typed measurements to the rescue!

Working in typed measurements increases safety by dealing with what you really care about: units of measure.

Conversions to and from different units are simple, and operator overrides allow you to work with the measurements directly.

### Currently available measurement types

- Acceleration
- Angle
- Angular Velocity
- Area
- Current
- Data (bytes, etc)
- Density
- Energy
- Force
- Frequency
- Length
- Humidity
- Mass
- Power
- Pressure
- Resistance
- Speed
- Temperature
- Torque
- Voltage
- Volume

### Examples

In your Cargo.toml add the dependency...

```
[]
 = "0.11"
```
In your code...

```
use ;
```
### Features

The crate contains few features to disable or enable certain functionalities:

- `std`- Enables functionality that Rust standard library provides instead of using `libm`for some math functions

- Enables functionality that Rust standard library provides instead of using
- from_str
- Allows creating measurement units from string input

**References**

I am by no means a measurement or math expert, I simply wanted to do something useful while learning Rust. Thank you to these sites and their authors for the great reference material used in building this library.

---

# measurements - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/measurements/0.11.1/target-redirect/measurements/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#measurements)Measurements

Measurements is a crate that lets you represent physical quantities, such as Lengths, Masses, Pressures, etc. Each quantity has a series of functions that allow you to convert to and from common units. You can also perform arithmetic on the quantities - for example you can divide a Force by an Area to get a Pressure.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use length::`- [Distance](https://docs.rs/length/type.Distance.html);

[153](#153)impl Measurement for time::Duration {
[154](#154)    fn get_base_units_name(&self) -> &'static str {
[155](#155)        "s"
[156](#156)    }
[157](#157)
[158](#158)    fn as_base_units(&self) -> f64 {
[159](#159)        self.as_secs() as f64 + (f64::from(self.subsec_nanos()) * 1e-9)
[160](#160)    }
[161](#161)
[162](#162)    fn from_base_units(units: f64) -> Self {
[163](#163)        let subsec_nanos = ((units * 1e9) % 1e9) as u32;
[164](#164)        let secs = units as u64;
[165](#165)        time::Duration::new(secs, subsec_nanos)
[166](#166)    }
[167](#167)}

# Length in measurements::length - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/length/struct.Length.html

`pub struct Length { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The Length struct can be used to deal with lengths in a common way. Common metric and imperial units are supported.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use measurements::Length;
let football_field = Length::from_yards(100.0);
let meters = football_field.as_meters();
println!("There are {} meters in a football field.", meters);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/measurements/length.rs.html#58-60)#### pub fn [from_meters](https://docs.rs#method.from_meters)(meters: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f64.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/measurements/length.rs.html#58-60)

#### pub fn [from_meters](https://docs.rs#method.from_meters)(meters: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f64.html)) -> Self

Create a new Length from a floating point value in meters

```
3fn main() {
4    for power in -12..12 {
5        let val: f64 = 123.456 * (10f64.powf(f64::from(power)));
6        println!("10^{}...", power);
7        println!("Temp of {0:.3} outside", Temperature::from_kelvin(val));
8        println!("Distance of {0:.3}", Length::from_meters(val));
9        println!("Pressure of {0:.3}", Pressure::from_millibars(val));
10        println!("Volume of {0:.3}", Volume::from_litres(val));
11        println!("Mass of {0:.3}", Mass::from_kilograms(val));
12        println!("Speed of {0:.3}", Speed::from_meters_per_second(val));
13        println!(
14            "Acceleration of {0:.3}",
15            Acceleration::from_meters_per_second_per_second(val)
16        );
17        println!("Energy of {0:.3}", Energy::from_joules(val));
18        println!("Power of {0:.3}", Power::from_watts(val));
19        println!("Force of {0:.3}", Force::from_newtons(val));
20        println!("Force of {0:.3}", Torque::from_newton_metres(val));
21        println!(
22            "Force of {0:.3}",
23            AngularVelocity::from_radians_per_second(val)
24        );
25        println!("Data size is {0:.3}", Data::from_octets(val));
26    }
27}
```

#### pub fn [from_millimeters](https://docs.rs#method.from_millimeters)(millimeters: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f64.html)) -> Self

Create a new Length from a floating point value in millimeters.

```
1fn main() {
2    // Sinusiodal Oscilator moves at 5 Hz across 50 mm
3    let f = measurements::Frequency::from_hertz(5.0);
4    let d = measurements::Distance::from_millimeters(50.0);
5    // Speed = PI * Frequency * Displacement
6    // Speed = PI * Displacement / Period
7    let v = std::f64::consts::PI * d / f.as_period();
8    println!(
9        "Maximum speed of a pendulum at {:.1} with max displacement {:.1} is {:.1}",
10        f, d, v
11    );
12}
```

# Temperature in measurements::temperature - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/temperature/struct.Temperature.html

`pub struct Temperature { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The `Temperature` struct can be used to deal with absolute temperatures in
a common way.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use measurements::Temperature;
let boiling_water = Temperature::from_celsius(100.0);
let fahrenheit = boiling_water.as_fahrenheit();
println!("Boiling water measures at {} degrees fahrenheit.", fahrenheit);
```

Create a new Temperature from a floating point value in Kelvin

```
3fn main() {
4    for power in -12..12 {
5        let val: f64 = 123.456 * (10f64.powf(f64::from(power)));
6        println!("10^{}...", power);
7        println!("Temp of {0:.3} outside", Temperature::from_kelvin(val));
8        println!("Distance of {0:.3}", Length::from_meters(val));
9        println!("Pressure of {0:.3}", Pressure::from_millibars(val));
10        println!("Volume of {0:.3}", Volume::from_litres(val));
11        println!("Mass of {0:.3}", Mass::from_kilograms(val));
12        println!("Speed of {0:.3}", Speed::from_meters_per_second(val));
13        println!(
14            "Acceleration of {0:.3}",
15            Acceleration::from_meters_per_second_per_second(val)
16        );
17        println!("Energy of {0:.3}", Energy::from_joules(val));
18        println!("Power of {0:.3}", Power::from_watts(val));
19        println!("Force of {0:.3}", Force::from_newtons(val));
20        println!("Force of {0:.3}", Torque::from_newton_metres(val));
21        println!(
22            "Force of {0:.3}",
23            AngularVelocity::from_radians_per_second(val)
24        );
25        println!("Data size is {0:.3}", Data::from_octets(val));
26    }
27}
```

# TemperatureDelta in measurements::temperature - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/temperature/struct.TemperatureDelta.html

`pub struct TemperatureDelta { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The `TemperatureDelta` struct can be used to deal with differences between
temperatures in a common way.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use measurements::{Temperature, TemperatureDelta};
let boiling_water = Temperature::from_celsius(100.0);
let frozen_water = Temperature::from_celsius(0.0);
let difference: TemperatureDelta = boiling_water - frozen_water;
println!("Boiling water is {} above freezing.", difference);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# Humidity in measurements::humidity - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/humidity/struct.Humidity.html

`pub struct Humidity { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The `Humidity` struct can be used to deal with relative humidity
in air in a common way. Relative humidity is an important metric used
in weather forecasts.

Relative humidity (as a ratio and percentage) and conversions between relative humidity and dewpoint are supported. It also provides calculations giving vapour pressure and absolute humidity.

Relative humidity gives the ratio of how much moisture the air is holding to how much moisture it could hold at a given temperature. Here we use the technical definition of humidity as ratio of the actual water vapor pressure to the equilibrium vapor pressure (often called the “saturation” vapor pressure).

For dewpoint calculations, we use the algorithm commonly known as the Magnus formula, with coefficients derived by Alduchov and Eskridge (1996), which gives resonable accuracy (vapour pressure error < 0.2%) for temperatures between 0 deg C, and 50 deg C.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example:

```
    //  calculate the dewpoint from the relative humidity
    use measurements::{Humidity,Temperature};
    let humidity = Humidity::from_percent(85.0);
    let temp = Temperature::from_celsius(18.0);
    let dewpoint = humidity.as_dewpoint(temp);
    println!("At {} humidity, air at {} has a dewpoint of {}", humidity, temp, dewpoint);
```

# Mass in measurements::mass - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/mass/struct.Mass.html

`pub struct Mass { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The Mass struct can be used to deal with mass in a common way. Metric, avoirdupois imperial and troy imperial units are supported.

#Example

```
use measurements::Mass;
let metric_ton = Mass::from_metric_tons(1.0);
let united_states_tons = metric_ton.as_short_tons();
let united_states_pounds = metric_ton.as_pounds();
println!(
    "One metric ton is {} U.S. tons - that's {} pounds!",
    united_states_tons, united_states_pounds);
```

# Volume in measurements::volume - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/volume/struct.Volume.html

`pub struct Volume { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The `Volume` struct can be used to deal with volumes in a common way.

#Example

```
use measurements::Volume;
let gallon = Volume::from_gallons(1.0);
let pint = Volume::from_pints(1.0);
let beers = gallon / pint;
println!("A gallon of beer will pour {} pints!", beers);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

3fn main() {
4    for power in -12..12 {
5        let val: f64 = 123.456 * (10f64.powf(f64::from(power)));
6        println!("10^{}...", power);
7        println!("Temp of {0:.3} outside", Temperature::from_kelvin(val));
8        println!("Distance of {0:.3}", Length::from_meters(val));
9        println!("Pressure of {0:.3}", Pressure::from_millibars(val));
10        println!("Volume of {0:.3}", Volume::from_litres(val));
11        println!("Mass of {0:.3}", Mass::from_kilograms(val));
12        println!("Speed of {0:.3}", Speed::from_meters_per_second(val));
13        println!(
14            "Acceleration of {0:.3}",
15            Acceleration::from_meters_per_second_per_second(val)
16        );
17        println!("Energy of {0:.3}", Energy::from_joules(val));
18        println!("Power of {0:.3}", Power::from_watts(val));
19        println!("Force of {0:.3}", Force::from_newtons(val));
20        println!("Force of {0:.3}", Torque::from_newton_metres(val));
21        println!(
22            "Force of {0:.3}",
23            AngularVelocity::from_radians_per_second(val)
24        );
25        println!("Data size is {0:.3}", Data::from_octets(val));
26    }
27}
```

# Density in measurements::density - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/density/struct.Density.html

`pub struct Density { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The `Density` struct can be used to deal with Densities in a common way, to enable mass,
volume and density calculations and unit conversions.

[§](https://docs.rs#example1---calculating-volume-from-units-of-mass-and-density)Example1 - calculating volume from units of mass and density

```
use measurements::{Density, Mass, Volume};
// Q: A 12 stone man hops into a brimming full bath, completely emersing himself.
// How many gallons of water spill on the floor?
// (Assume The human body is roughly about as dense as water - 1 gm/cm³)
//
let body_density: Density = Mass::from_grams(1.0) / Volume:: from_cubic_centimetres(1.0);
let mans_weight = Mass::from_stones(12.0);
let water_volume = mans_weight / body_density;
println!("{} gallons of water spilled on the floor", water_volume.as_gallons());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example2---converting-to-ad-hoc-units-of-density)Example2 - converting to ad-hoc units of density

```
use measurements::{Density, Mass, Volume};
// Q: what is 3 grams per litre in units of ounces per quart?
//
let density: Density = Mass::from_grams(3.0) / Volume:: from_litres(1.0);
let ounces = (density * Volume::from_quarts(1.0)).as_ounces();
println!("Answer is {} ounces per quart", ounces);
```

# Pressure in measurements::pressure - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/pressure/struct.Pressure.html

`pub struct Pressure { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The `Pressure` struct can be used to deal with pressures in a common way.
Common metric and imperial units are supported.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use measurements::Pressure;
let earth = Pressure::from_atmospheres(1.0);
let mbar = earth.as_millibars();
println!("Atmospheric pressure is {} mbar.", mbar);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create new Pressure from floating point value in millibars (mBar)

```
3fn main() {
4    for power in -12..12 {
5        let val: f64 = 123.456 * (10f64.powf(f64::from(power)));
6        println!("10^{}...", power);
7        println!("Temp of {0:.3} outside", Temperature::from_kelvin(val));
8        println!("Distance of {0:.3}", Length::from_meters(val));
9        println!("Pressure of {0:.3}", Pressure::from_millibars(val));
10        println!("Volume of {0:.3}", Volume::from_litres(val));
11        println!("Mass of {0:.3}", Mass::from_kilograms(val));
12        println!("Speed of {0:.3}", Speed::from_meters_per_second(val));
13        println!(
14            "Acceleration of {0:.3}",
15            Acceleration::from_meters_per_second_per_second(val)
16        );
17        println!("Energy of {0:.3}", Energy::from_joules(val));
18        println!("Power of {0:.3}", Power::from_watts(val));
19        println!("Force of {0:.3}", Force::from_newtons(val));
20        println!("Force of {0:.3}", Torque::from_newton_metres(val));
21        println!(
22            "Force of {0:.3}",
23            AngularVelocity::from_radians_per_second(val)
24        );
25        println!("Data size is {0:.3}", Data::from_octets(val));
26    }
27}
```

`pub struct Speed { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The `Speed` struct can be used to deal with speeds in a common way.
Common metric and imperial units are supported.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use measurements::Speed;
let light = Speed::from_meters_per_second(300_000_000.0);

# Acceleration in measurements::acceleration - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/acceleration/struct.Acceleration.html

`pub struct Acceleration { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The `Acceleration` struct can be used to deal with Accelerations in a common way.
Common metric and imperial units are supported.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use measurements::{Acceleration, Length, Speed};
use std::time::Duration;
fn main() {
    // Standing quarter mile in 10.0 dead, at 120.0 mph
    let track = Length::from_miles(0.25);
    let finish = Speed::from_miles_per_hour(120.0);
    let time = Duration::new(10, 0);
    let accel: Acceleration = finish / time;
    println!("You accelerated over {} at an average of {}", track, accel);
}
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create a new Acceleration from a floating point value in meters per second per second

```
3fn main() {
4    for power in -12..12 {
5        let val: f64 = 123.456 * (10f64.powf(f64::from(power)));
6        println!("10^{}...", power);
7        println!("Temp of {0:.3} outside", Temperature::from_kelvin(val));
8        println!("Distance of {0:.3}", Length::from_meters(val));
9        println!("Pressure of {0:.3}", Pressure::from_millibars(val));
10        println!("Volume of {0:.3}", Volume::from_litres(val));
11        println!("Mass of {0:.3}", Mass::from_kilograms(val));
12        println!("Speed of {0:.3}", Speed::from_meters_per_second(val));
13        println!(
14            "Acceleration of {0:.3}",
15            Acceleration::from_meters_per_second_per_second(val)
16        );
17        println!("Energy of {0:.3}", Energy::from_joules(val));
18        println!("Power of {0:.3}", Power::from_watts(val));
19        println!("Force of {0:.3}", Force::from_newtons(val));
20        println!("Force of {0:.3}", Torque::from_newton_metres(val));
21        println!(
22            "Force of {0:.3}",
23            AngularVelocity::from_radians_per_second(val)
24        );
25        println!("Data size is {0:.3}", Data::from_octets(val));
26    }
27}
```

```
3fn main() {
4    let power = Power::from_ps(225.0);
5    let peak_revs = AngularVelocity::from_rpm(6000.0);
6    let torque = power / peak_revs;
7    println!(
8        "At {:.0} rpm, a {:.1} ({:.1} PS) engine, produces {:.1} ({:.1} lbf·ft)",
9        peak_revs.as_rpm(),
10        power,
11        power.as_ps(),
12        torque,
13        torque.as_pound_foot()
14    );
15}
```

`pub struct Voltage { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

in a common way.

use measurements::Voltage;

let k_v = volts.as_kilovolts();

# Force in measurements::force - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/force/struct.Force.html

`pub struct Force { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The `Force` struct can be used to deal with force in a common way.

#Example

```
use measurements::Force;
use measurements::Mass;
use measurements::Acceleration;
let metric_ton = Mass::from_metric_tons(1.0);
let gravity = Acceleration::from_meters_per_second_per_second(9.81);
let force: Force = metric_ton * gravity; // F=ma
println!(
    "One metric ton exerts a force of {} due to gravity",
    force);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/measurements/force.rs.html#39-41)#### pub fn [from_newtons](https://docs.rs#method.from_newtons)(newtons: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f64.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/measurements/force.rs.html#39-41)

#### pub fn [from_newtons](https://docs.rs#method.from_newtons)(newtons: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f64.html)) -> Self

Create a Force from a floating point value in Newtons

```
3fn main() {
4    for power in -12..12 {
5        let val: f64 = 123.456 * (10f64.powf(f64::from(power)));
6        println!("10^{}...", power);
7        println!("Temp of {0:.3} outside", Temperature::from_kelvin(val));
8        println!("Distance of {0:.3}", Length::from_meters(val));
9        println!("Pressure of {0:.3}", Pressure::from_millibars(val));
10        println!("Volume of {0:.3}", Volume::from_litres(val));
11        println!("Mass of {0:.3}", Mass::from_kilograms(val));
12        println!("Speed of {0:.3}", Speed::from_meters_per_second(val));
13        println!(
14            "Acceleration of {0:.3}",
15            Acceleration::from_meters_per_second_per_second(val)
16        );
17        println!("Energy of {0:.3}", Energy::from_joules(val));
18        println!("Power of {0:.3}", Power::from_watts(val));
19        println!("Force of {0:.3}", Force::from_newtons(val));
20        println!("Force of {0:.3}", Torque::from_newton_metres(val));
21        println!(
22            "Force of {0:.3}",
23            AngularVelocity::from_radians_per_second(val)
24        );
25        println!("Data size is {0:.3}", Data::from_octets(val));
26    }
27}
```

# Area in measurements::area - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/area/struct.Area.html

`pub struct Area { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The `Area` struct can be used to deal with areas in a common way.
Common metric and imperial units are supported.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use measurements::Area;
let football_field = Area::from_square_meters(7140.0);
let acres = football_field.as_acres();
println!("There are {} acres in a football field.", acres);
```

# Angle in measurements::angle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/angle/struct.Angle.html

`pub struct Angle { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The ‘Angle’ struct can be used to deal with angles in a common way.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use measurements::Angle;
let whole_cake = Angle::from_degrees(360.0);
let pieces = 6.0;
let slice = whole_cake / pieces;
println!("Each slice will be {} degrees", slice.as_degrees());
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Returns a string containing the most appropriate units for this quantity,
and a floating point value representing this quantity in those units.
Useful when, for example, a length might be in millimeters if it is very small,
or kilometers when it is very large.

# Frequency in measurements::frequency - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/frequency/struct.Frequency.html

`pub struct Frequency { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The Frequency struct can be used to deal with frequencies in a common way. Common SI prefixes are supported.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use measurements::Frequency;
let radio_station = Frequency::from_hertz(101.5e6);
println!("Tune to {}.", radio_station);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/measurements/frequency.rs.html#43-45)#### pub fn [from_hertz](https://docs.rs#method.from_hertz)(hertz: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f64.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/measurements/frequency.rs.html#43-45)

#### pub fn [from_hertz](https://docs.rs#method.from_hertz)(hertz: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f64.html)) -> Self

Create a new Frequency from a floating point value in hertz

```
1fn main() {
2    // Sinusiodal Oscilator moves at 5 Hz across 50 mm
3    let f = measurements::Frequency::from_hertz(5.0);
4    let d = measurements::Distance::from_millimeters(50.0);
5    // Speed = PI * Frequency * Displacement
6    // Speed = PI * Displacement / Period
7    let v = std::f64::consts::PI * d / f.as_period();
8    println!(
9        "Maximum speed of a pendulum at {:.1} with max displacement {:.1} is {:.1}",
10        f, d, v
11    );
12}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/measurements/frequency.rs.html#48-50)#### pub fn [from_nanohertz](https://docs.rs#method.from_nanohertz)(nanohertz: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f64.html)) -> Self

Convert this Frequency to a floating point value of the period in seconds.

```
1fn main() {
2    // Sinusiodal Oscilator moves at 5 Hz across 50 mm
3    let f = measurements::Frequency::from_hertz(5.0);
4    let d = measurements::Distance::from_millimeters(50.0);
5    // Speed = PI * Frequency * Displacement
6    // Speed = PI * Displacement / Period
7    let v = std::f64::consts::PI * d / f.as_period();
8    println!(
9        "Maximum speed of a pendulum at {:.1} with max displacement {:.1} is {:.1}",
10        f, d, v
11    );
12}
```

# AngularVelocity in measurements::angular_velocity - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/angular_velocity/struct.AngularVelocity.html

`pub struct AngularVelocity { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The ‘AngularVelocity’ struct can be used to deal with angular velocities in a common way.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use measurements::AngularVelocity;
const cylinders: f64 = 6.0;
let engine_speed = AngularVelocity::from_rpm(9000.0);
let sparks_per_second = (engine_speed.as_hertz() / 2.0) * cylinders;
```

18        println!("Power of {0:.3}", Power::from_watts(val));

20        println!("Force of {0:.3}", Torque::from_newton_metres(val));

Create a new AngularVelocity from a floating point value in revolutions per minute (RPM)

```
3fn main() {
4    let power = Power::from_ps(225.0);
5    let peak_revs = AngularVelocity::from_rpm(6000.0);
6    let torque = power / peak_revs;
7    println!(
8        "At {:.0} rpm, a {:.1} ({:.1} PS) engine, produces {:.1} ({:.1} lbf·ft)",
9        peak_revs.as_rpm(),
10        power,
11        power.as_ps(),
12        torque,
13        torque.as_pound_foot()
14    );
15}
```

6    let torque = power / peak_revs;
7    println!(
8        "At {:.0} rpm, a {:.1} ({:.1} PS) engine, produces {:.1} ({:.1} lbf·ft)",
9        peak_revs.as_rpm(),
10        power,
11        power.as_ps(),
12        torque,
13        torque.as_pound_foot()
14    );
15}
```

# Data in measurements::data - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/data/struct.Data.html

`pub struct Data { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The `Data` struct can be used to deal with computer information in a common way.
Common legacy and SI units are supported.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use measurements::Data;
let file_size = Data::from_mebioctets(2.5);
let octets = file_size.as_octets();
println!("There are {} octets in that file.", octets);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/measurements/data.rs.html#40-42)

#### pub fn [from_octets](https://docs.rs#method.from_octets)(octets: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f64.html)) -> Self

Create new Data from floating point value in Octets

```
3fn main() {
4    for power in -12..12 {
5        let val: f64 = 123.456 * (10f64.powf(f64::from(power)));
6        println!("10^{}...", power);
7        println!("Temp of {0:.3} outside", Temperature::from_kelvin(val));
8        println!("Distance of {0:.3}", Length::from_meters(val));
9        println!("Pressure of {0:.3}", Pressure::from_millibars(val));
10        println!("Volume of {0:.3}", Volume::from_litres(val));
11        println!("Mass of {0:.3}", Mass::from_kilograms(val));
12        println!("Speed of {0:.3}", Speed::from_meters_per_second(val));
13        println!(
14            "Acceleration of {0:.3}",
15            Acceleration::from_meters_per_second_per_second(val)
16        );
17        println!("Energy of {0:.3}", Energy::from_joules(val));
18        println!("Power of {0:.3}", Power::from_watts(val));
19        println!("Force of {0:.3}", Force::from_newtons(val));
20        println!("Force of {0:.3}", Torque::from_newton_metres(val));
21        println!(
22            "Force of {0:.3}",
23            AngularVelocity::from_radians_per_second(val)
24        );
25        println!("Data size is {0:.3}", Data::from_octets(val));
26    }
27}
```

# TorqueEnergy in measurements - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/struct.TorqueEnergy.html

`pub struct TorqueEnergy { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

If you multiply a Force by a Length, we can’t tell if you’re pushing something along (which requires Energy) or rotating something (which creates a Torque). This struct is what results from the multiplication, and you have to then convert it to whichever you want.

# Measurement in measurements - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/0.11.1/measurements/trait.Measurement.html

```
pub trait Measurement {
    // Required methods
    fn
```
[get_base_units_name](https://docs.rs#tymethod.get_base_units_name)(&self) -> &'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.str.html);
[as_base_units](https://docs.rs#tymethod.as_base_units)(&self) -> [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f64.html);
[from_base_units](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_base_units)(units: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f64.html)) -> Self;
    // Provided methods
    fn [get_appropriate_units](https://docs.rs#method.get_appropriate_units)(&self) -> (&'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.str.html), [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f64.html)) { ... }
[pick_appropriate_units](https://docs.rs#method.pick_appropriate_units)(
        &self,
        list: &[(&'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.str.html), [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f64.html))],
    ) -> (&'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.str.html), [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f64.html)) { ... }
}## Expand description

All measurements implement this.

It provides conversion functions to and from raw numbers.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// Importing the `implement_display` and `implement_measurement` macros from the `measurements` crate
use measurements::{implement_display, implement_measurement, Measurement};
struct Cubits {
    forearms: f64
}
impl Measurement for Cubits {
    fn as_base_units(&self) -> f64 {
        self.forearms
    }
    fn from_base_units(units: f64) -> Self {
        Cubits { forearms: units }
    }
   fn get_base_units_name(&self) -> &'static str {
       "cu"
   }
}
// Invoke the macro to automatically implement Add, Sub, etc...
implement_measurement! { Cubits }
// The main function here is only included to make doc test_utils compile.
// You should't need it in your own code.
fn main() { }
```
## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/measurements/measurement.rs.html#47-49)#### fn [get_appropriate_units](https://docs.rs#method.get_appropriate_units)(&self) -> (&'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.str.html), [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f64.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/measurements/measurement.rs.html#47-49)

#### fn [get_appropriate_units](https://docs.rs#method.get_appropriate_units)(&self) -> (&'static [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.str.html), [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f64.html))

Returns a string containing the most appropriate units for this quantity, and a floating point value representing this quantity in those units. Useful when, for example, a length might be in millimeters if it is very small, or kilometers when it is very large.

The default implementation always selects the base unit. Override in your Measurement impl to select better units if required.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# measurements - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/measurements/latest/measurements/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#measurements)Measurements

Measurements is a crate that lets you represent physical quantities, such as Lengths, Masses, Pressures, etc. Each quantity has a series of functions that allow you to convert to and from common units. You can also perform arithmetic on the quantities - for example you can divide a Force by an Area to get a Pressure.

- This is a special macro that creates the code to implement operator and comparison overrides.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Torque](https://docs.rs/struct.TorqueEnergy.html)- Energy
- If you multiply a Force by a Length, we can’t tell if you’re pushing something along (which requires Energy) or rotating something (which creates a Torque). This struct is what results from the multiplication, and you have to then convert it to whichever you want.

- All measurements implement this.

needs, there is no need to add

`libm` as a dependency.If more functionality is needed, this crate can also be used directly:

 = "0.2.11"

# regex 1.12.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/regex/^1

# regex

This crate provides routines for searching strings for matches of a [regular
expression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_expression) (aka "regex"). The regex syntax supported by this crate is similar
to other regex engines, but it lacks several features that are not known how to
implement efficiently. This includes, but is not limited to, look-around and
backreferences. In exchange, all regex searches in this crate have worst case
`O(m * n)` time complexity, where `m` is proportional to the size of the regex
and `n` is proportional to the size of the string being searched.

### Documentation

[Module documentation with examples](https://docs.rs/regex).
The module documentation also includes a comprehensive description of the
syntax supported.

Documentation with examples for the various matching functions and iterators
can be found on the
[ Regex type](https://docs.rs/regex/*/regex/struct.Regex.html).

### Usage

To bring this crate into your repository, either add `regex` to your
`Cargo.toml`, or run `cargo add regex`.

Here's a simple example that matches a date in YYYY-MM-DD format and prints the year, month and day:

```
use Regex;
```
If you have lots of dates in text that you'd like to iterate over, then it's easy to adapt the above example with an iterator:

```
use Regex;
```
### Usage: Avoid compiling the same regex in a loop

It is an anti-pattern to compile the same regular expression in a loop since
compilation is typically expensive. (It takes anywhere from a few microseconds
to a few **milliseconds** depending on the size of the regex.) Not only is
compilation itself expensive, but this also prevents optimizations that reuse
allocations internally to the matching engines.

In Rust, it can sometimes be a pain to pass regular expressions around if
they're used from inside a helper function. Instead, we recommend using
[ std::sync::LazyLock](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/sync/struct.LazyLock.html), or the

[crate, if you can't use the standard library.](https://crates.io/crates/once_cell)

`once_cell`This example shows how to use `std::sync::LazyLock`:

```
use LazyLock;
use Regex;
```
Specifically, in this example, the regex will be compiled when it is used for the first time. On subsequent uses, it will reuse the previous compilation.

### Usage: match regular expressions on `&[u8]`

The main API of this crate (`regex::Regex`) requires the caller to pass a
`&str` for searching. In Rust, an `&str` is required to be valid UTF-8, which
means the main API can't be used for searching arbitrary bytes.

To match on arbitrary bytes, use the `regex::bytes::Regex` API. The API is
identical to the main API, except that it takes an `&[u8]` to search on instead
of an `&str`. The `&[u8]` APIs also permit disabling Unicode mode in the regex
even when the pattern would match invalid UTF-8. For example, `(?-u:.)` is
not allowed in `regex::Regex` but is allowed in `regex::bytes::Regex` since
`(?-u:.)` matches any byte except for `\n`. Conversely, `.` will match the
UTF-8 encoding of any Unicode scalar value except for `\n`.

This example shows how to find all null-terminated strings in a slice of bytes:

```
use Regex;
let re = new.unwrap;
let text = b"foo\xFFbar\x00baz\x00";
// Extract all of the strings without the null terminator from each match.
// The unwrap is OK here since a match requires the `cstr` capture to match.
let cstrs:  =
    re.captures_iter
      .map
      .collect;
assert_eq!;
```
Notice here that the `[^\x00]+` will match any *byte* except for `NUL`,
including bytes like `\xFF` which are not valid UTF-8. When using the main API,
`[^\x00]+` would instead match any valid UTF-8 sequence except for `NUL`.

### Usage: match multiple regular expressions simultaneously

This demonstrates how to use a `RegexSet` to match multiple (possibly
overlapping) regular expressions in a single scan of the search text:

```
use RegexSet;
let set = new.unwrap;
// Iterate over and collect all of the matches.
let matches:  = set.matches.into_iter.collect;
assert_eq!;
// You can also test whether a particular regex matched:
let matches = set.matches;
assert!;
assert!;
```
### Usage: regex internals as a library

The [ regex-automata directory](https://docs.rs/regex-automata/) contains a crate that
exposes all the internal matching engines used by the

`regex` crate. The
idea is that the `regex` crate exposes a simple API for 99% of use cases, but
`regex-automata` exposes oodles of customizable behaviors.### Usage: a regular expression parser

This repository contains a crate that provides a well tested regular expression parser, abstract syntax and a high-level intermediate representation for convenient analysis. It provides no facilities for compilation or execution. This may be useful if you're implementing your own regex engine or otherwise need to do analysis on the syntax of a regular expression. It is otherwise not recommended for general use.

### Crate features

This crate comes with several features that permit tweaking the trade-off between binary size, compilation time and runtime performance. Users of this crate can selectively disable Unicode tables, or choose from a variety of optimizations performed by this crate to disable.

When all of these features are disabled, runtime match performance may be much
worse, but if you're matching on short strings, or if high performance isn't
necessary, then such a configuration is perfectly serviceable. To disable
all such features, use the following `Cargo.toml` dependency configuration:

```
[]
 = "1.3"
 = false
# Unless you have a specific reason not to, it's good sense to enable standard
# library support. It enables several optimizations and avoids spin locks. It
# also shouldn't meaningfully impact compile times or binary size.
 = ["std"]
```
This will reduce the dependency tree of `regex` down to two crates:
`regex-syntax` and `regex-automata`.

The full set of features one can disable are
[in the "Crate features" section of the documentation](https://docs.rs/regex/1.*/#crate-features).

### Performance

One of the goals of this crate is for the regex engine to be "fast." What that
is a somewhat nebulous goal, it is usually interpreted in one of two ways.
First, it means that all searches take worst case `O(m * n)` time, where
`m` is proportional to `len(regex)` and `n` is proportional to `len(haystack)`.
Second, it means that even aside from the time complexity constraint, regex
searches are "fast" in practice.

While the first interpretation is pretty unambiguous, the second one remains nebulous. While nebulous, it guides this crate's architecture and the sorts of the trade-offs it makes. For example, here are some general architectural statements that follow as a result of the goal to be "fast":

- When given the choice between faster regex searches and faster *Rust compile times*, this crate will generally choose faster regex searches.
- When given the choice between faster regex searches and faster *regex compile times*, this crate will generally choose faster regex searches. That is, it is generally acceptable for`Regex::new`to get a little slower if it means that searches get faster. (This is a somewhat delicate balance to strike, because the speed of`Regex::new`needs to remain somewhat reasonable. But this is why one should avoid re-compiling the same regex over and over again.)
- When given the choice between faster regex searches and simpler API
design, this crate will generally choose faster regex searches. For example,
if one didn't care about performance, we could like get rid of both of
the `Regex::is_match`and`Regex::find`APIs and instead just rely on`Regex::captures`.

There are perhaps more ways that being "fast" influences things.

While this repository used to provide its own benchmark suite, it has since
been moved to [rebar](https://github.com/BurntSushi/rebar). The benchmarks are
quite extensive, and there are many more than what is shown in rebar's README
(which is just limited to a "curated" set meant to compare performance between
regex engines). To run all of this crate's benchmarks, first start by cloning
and installing `rebar`:

```
$ git clone https://github.com/BurntSushi/rebar
$ cd rebar
$ cargo install --path ./
```
Then build the benchmark harness for just this crate:

```
$ rebar build -e '^rust/regex$'
```
Run all benchmarks for this crate as tests (each benchmark is executed once to ensure it works):

```
$ rebar measure -e '^rust/regex$' -t
```
Record measurements for all benchmarks and save them to a CSV file:

```
$ rebar measure -e '^rust/regex$' | tee results.csv
```
Explore benchmark timings:

```
$ rebar cmp results.csv
```
See the `rebar` documentation for more details on how it works and how to
compare results with other regex engines.

### Hacking

The `regex` crate is, for the most part, a pretty thin wrapper around the
[ meta::Regex](https://docs.rs/regex-automata/latest/regex_automata/meta/struct.Regex.html)
from the

[. Therefore, if you're looking to work on the internals of this crate, you'll likely either want to look in](https://docs.rs/regex-automata/latest/regex_automata/)

`regex-automata` crate`regex-syntax` (for parsing) or `regex-automata`
(for construction of finite automata and the search routines).My [blog on regex internals](https://burntsushi.net/regex-internals/)
goes into more depth.

### Minimum Rust version policy

This crate's minimum supported `rustc` version is `1.65.0`.

The policy is that the minimum Rust version required to use this crate can be
increased in minor version updates. For example, if regex 1.0 requires Rust
1.20.0, then regex 1.0.z for all values of `z` will also require Rust 1.20.0 or
newer. However, regex 1.y for `y > 0` may require a newer minimum version of
Rust.

### License

This project is licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0, ([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

at your option.

The data in `regex-syntax/src/unicode_tables/` is licensed under the Unicode
License Agreement
([LICENSE-UNICODE](https://www.unicode.org/copyright.html#License)).

# measurements 0.11.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/measurements/0.11.0

# Type-safe units of measure for Rust

### Why should I care? I already have numbers...

Working with units can be very error prone. If one person is working in feet and one person is working in meters, what happens?

Doing all of your math in raw numerical types can be unsafe and downright confusing. What can we do to help?

### Typed measurements to the rescue!

Working in typed measurements increases safety by dealing with what you really care about: units of measure.

Conversions to and from different units are simple, and operator overrides allow you to work with the measurements directly.

### Currently available measurement types

- Acceleration
- Angle
- Angular Velocity
- Area
- Current
- Data (bytes, etc)
- Density
- Energy
- Force
- Frequency
- Length
- Humidity
- Mass
- Power
- Pressure
- Resistance
- Speed
- Temperature
- Torque
- Voltage
- Volume

### Examples

In your Cargo.toml add the dependency...

```
[]
 = "0.11"
```
In your code...

```
extern crate measurements;
use ;
```
### Features

The crate contains few features to disable or enable certain functionalities:

- `std`- Enables functionality that Rust standard library provides instead of using `libm`for some math functions

- Enables functionality that Rust standard library provides instead of using
- from_str
- Allows creating measurement units from string input

**References**

I am by no means a measurement or math expert, I simply wanted to do something useful while learning Rust. Thank you to these sites and their authors for the great reference material used in building this library.

---

# measurements 0.10.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/measurements/0.10.3

# Type-safe units of measure for Rust

### Why should I care? I already have numbers...

Working with units can be very error prone. If one person is working in feet and one person is working in meters, what happens?

Doing all of your math in raw numerical types can be unsafe and downright confusing. What can we do to help?

### Typed measurements to the rescue!

Working in typed measurements increases safety by dealing with what you really care about: units of measure.

Conversions to and from different units are simple, and operator overrides allow you to work with the measurements directly.

### Currently available measurement types

- Acceleration
- Angle
- Angular Velocity
- Area
- Current
- Data (bytes, etc)
- Energy
- Force
- Frequency
- Length
- Mass
- Power
- Pressure
- Resistance
- Speed
- Temperature
- Torque
- Voltage
- Volume

### Examples

In your Cargo.toml add the dependency...

```
[]
 = "^0.9.0"
```
In your code...

```
extern crate measurements;
use ;
```
**References**

I am by no means a measurement or math expert, I simply wanted to do something useful while learning Rust. Thank you to these sites and their authors for the great reference material used in building this library.

---

# measurements 0.2.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/measurements/0.2.1

# Type-safe units of measure for Rust

### Why should I care? I already have numbers...

Working with units can be very error prone. If one person is working in feet and one person is working in meters, what happens?

Doing all of your math in raw numerical types can be unsafe and downright confusing. What can we do to help?

### Typed measurements to the rescue!

Working in typed measurements increases safety by dealing with what you really care about: units of measure.

Conversions to and from different units are simple, and operator overrides allow you to work with the measurements directly.

### Currently available measurement types

- Length
- Temperature
- Weight
- Volume

### Examples

In your Cargo.toml add the dependency...

```
[dependencies]
measurements = "^0.2.1"
```
In your code...

```
extern crate measurements;
use ;
// Lengths!
let football_field = from_yards;
let meters = football_field.as_meters;
println!;
/// Temperatures!
let boiling_water = from_celsius;
let fahrenheit = boiling_water.as_fahrenheit;
println!;
// Weights!
let metric_ton = from_metric_tons;
let united_states_tons = metric_ton.as_short_tons;
let united_states_pounds = metric_ton.as_pounds;
println!;
// Volumes!
let gallon = from_gallons;
let pint = from_pints;
let beers = gallon / pint;
println!;
```
**References**

I am by no means a measurement or math expert, I simply wanted to do something useful while learning Rust. Thank you to these sites and their authors for the great reference material used in building this library.

---

# measurements 0.2.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/measurements/0.2.0

# And Rust said, "Let there be units".

Hurray! Now you can work with units of measure in a headache-free way.

Currently available units:

- Length
- Temperature
- Weight

### Example

In your Cargo.toml...

```
[dependencies]
measurements = "^0.2.0"
```
In your code...

```
extern crate measurements;
use ;
let football_field = from_yards;
let meters = football_field.as_meters;
println!;
let boiling_water = from_celsius;
let fahrenheit = boiling_water.as_fahrenheit;
println!;
let metric_ton = from_metric_tons;
let united_states_tons = metric_ton.as_short_tons;
let united_states_pounds = metric_ton.as_pounds;
println!;
```
**References**

I am by no means a measurement or math expert, I simply wanted to do something useful while learning Rust. Thank you to these sites and their authors for the great reference material used in building this library.

---

# measurements 0.1.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/measurements/0.1.0

# And Rust said, "Let there be units."

Hurray! Now you can work with units of measure in a headache-free way.

Currently only `Length` is available, but I am planning to add more shortly.

### Example

```
let football_field = Length::from_yards(1.0);
let meters = football_field.as_meters();
println!("There are {} meters in a football field.", meters);
```

# measurements 0.11.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/measurements/latest/source/CHANGELOG.md

#ChangelogAll notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.
The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](http://keepachangelog.com/en/1.0.0/)
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](http://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).
##[Unreleased]##[0.11.1]##Added-Derive `Default` for all measurement structs
- Accept `lb` as a synonym for `lbs` for mass.
- Torr, milliTorr and mmHg as units of pressure
##[0.11.0]###Changed-Replaced the `no_std` feature with an additive `std` feature, fixing problems with serde serialization on `no_std` targets.
##[0.10.4]###Added-Humidity and density in [#27](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/rust-measurements/pull/27)- Support for parsing many values from strings.
###Changed-Merged in [#36](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/rust-measurements/pull/36) to adjust bounds on `Measurements::pick_appropriate_units()`, which changes the return value for cases when the value is 1.0.
- More accurate factors for meter to inch, feet, yard, furlong, mile.
##[0.10.3]###Added-This Changelog.
- Serde support.
##[0.10.2]
Merged in [#17](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/rust-measurements/pull/17) to add:
*nanoamps
* microwatts
* milliwatts
* microvolts
##[0.10.1]
The tests now work correctly after the `#[no_std]` move.
##[0.10.0]
Now builds for `#[no_std]` targets.
##[0.9.0]
Adds:
*Electrical Current (in Amps)
* Electrical Resistance (in Ohms)
* Corresponding updates to Power and Voltage
##[0.8.0]
Added the Voltage type, in Volts.
##[0.7.0]
Uses the [time](https://crates.io/crates/time) crate, to avoid `std::time` (which isn't available with `#[no_std]`).
##[0.6.0]
Adds:
*Angles
* Angular Velocity
* Area
* Data (bytes, etc)
* Force
* Frequency
* Mass
* Metric Horsepower (PS)
Changed Pressure to be in Pascals. Also add a bunch of tests and doc fixes.

# measurements 0.11.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/measurements/latest/source/clippy.toml

#
                    measurements 0.11.1

                Handle metric, imperial, and other measurements with ease! Types: Length, Temperature, Weight, Volume, Pressure

---

# measurements 0.11.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/measurements/latest/source/README.md

```
[![Build Status](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/rust-measurements/workflows/Build/badge.svg)](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/rust-measurements/actions?query=workflow%3ABuild)
Working with units can be very error prone.
If one person is working in feet and one person is working in meters, what happens?
Doing all of your math in raw numerical types can be unsafe and downright confusing.
What can we do to help?
Working in typed measurements increases safety by dealing with what you really care about: units of measure.
Conversions to and from different units are simple, and operator overrides allow you to work with the measurements directly.
- --------------------
In your Cargo.toml add the dependency...
```toml
[dependencies]
measurements = "0.11"
```
In your code...
```rust
use measurements::{Length, Pressure, Temperature, Volume, Mass};
fn main() {
}
```
The crate contains few features to disable or enable certain functionalities:
*     **    *
**References**
I am by no means a measurement or math expert, I simply wanted to do something useful while learning Rust. Thank you to these sites and their authors for the great reference material used in building this library.
  -   -
```

# libm 0.2.16 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/libm/0.2.16

`libm`

A Rust implementations of the C math library.

## Usage

`libm` provides fallback implementations for Rust's [float math functions](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/primitive.f32.html) in
`core`, and the [ core_float_math](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/137578) feature. If what is available suits your
needs, there is no need to add

`libm` as a dependency.If more functionality is needed, this crate can also be used directly:

```
[]
 = "0.2.11"
```

Please check [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://docs.rs/CONTRIBUTING.md)
